name: MandaABoa
tagline: A small Portuguese-language web utility sold as a self-serve subscription, the kind of single-purpose tool that lives or dies on its landing page.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Tools in this shape are usually one form, one database table, and one generated artifact, which is squarely inside what a coding agent does well in a single sitting. The catch is scoping: the public footprint here is thin enough that you cannot write a precise spec without clicking through the product yourself, and a vague spec is how one-shot builds turn into three-day builds. If the core loop is as narrow as it looks, a local Next.js plus SQLite version gets you most of the way before dinner. If it turns out to hang off a messaging API, a payment rail, or a deliverability pipeline, the build stops being a weekend and starts being an ops problem. Treat the verdict as provisional until someone has actually used the thing.
coreLoopDIY: Runs a local web app where you submit the input, it stores it in SQLite, and it renders the shareable output page or export you were paying for.
requirements: A local SQLite file, no database server
A place to host it if you want the output links to be public
whatYouLose: Someone else's uptime, backups, and domain, so your links do not rot when your laptop sleeps
A mobile-friendly, already-debugged UI instead of whatever your agent emits on the first pass
Any integration the hosted product has with messaging, payment, or delivery providers
Support in Portuguese from people who understand the local workflow the tool was built around
Whatever features exist behind the login that you never saw and therefore never specified
moatNotes: Narrow regional utilities compete on knowing one workflow very well, not on technology. That is real, but it is not a moat against a build you only need to work for you.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the subscription is almost certainly cheaper than an afternoon of your time, and because the hosted version keeps working when you are not looking at it. Small regional tools also tend to encode a specific local habit, a form layout, a phrasing, a legal nicety, that a generic clone silently gets wrong. If the thing already sits in your routine and costs less than lunch, replacing it is a hobby, not a saving.
notes: Thin public footprint, so the estimate assumes the obvious core loop and nothing clever hiding behind the login.
prompt:
Build a local, single-purpose web utility that replaces a small self-serve SaaS tool. No accounts, no billing, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind.
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/app.db, migrations as plain SQL in ./migrations run on boot.
- Server actions for writes. No tRPC, no Prisma, no auth library.

Core loop:
1. A single form page at / with the inputs the tool takes. Start with: title, body text, optional recipient name, optional date. Keep the field list in one config file (src/fields.ts) so I can edit it in one place.
2. Submitting stores a row in SQLite with a nanoid public id and a created_at timestamp.
3. Each row gets a rendered output page at /v/[id]: clean, mobile-first, printable, with a copy-link button.
4. /list shows every row with search by title, newest first, delete with confirm, and a "Download CSV" button that exports all rows.

In scope:
- Zod validation on the server action, inline field errors.
- Empty states and a 404 page for unknown ids.
- A seed script (npm run seed) that inserts three example rows.
- README with run steps and a note that data lives in ./data/app.db and should be backed up.

Out of scope, do not build:
- Login, multi-tenancy, roles, Stripe, email sending, SMS or WhatsApp sending, analytics, Docker, tests beyond a smoke check.

Rules:
- Any secret goes in .env.example with empty values, never hardcoded. The app must run with no secrets set.
- No external API calls at runtime.
- Finish with a working npm run dev and nothing in the console.
